method: Each listed item was read with its stem, all options, keyed answer(s), explanations and takeaway. Statuses are manually reasoned, not inferred from a schema or automated pass rule.
limitations: Independent AI editorial/clinical-reasoning screen; not external clinician validation or psychometric validation.
Pass applies only to the recorded content hash. New or changed content requires further review.
No comparison against proprietary examination items; originality judged from author provenance and item content.
Cross-bank learning-objective overlap remains provisional until all batches are available.
Source checks below support only the explicitly associated claims; other category references are general reading unless specifically verified.

sourceChecks.note: Current consent/autonomy standard opened earlier; supports collaborative preferences, not specific pain/terminal-care protocol.
Reduced-sensation heat avoidance supported by retrieved Diabetes Canada foot-care guidance.

items.assessment: Behavioural assessment with collateral history is correct, but no-pain-without-rating and family-picked-number distractors are caricatures.
issues: Behavioural assessment with collateral history is correct, but no-pain-without-rating and family-picked-number distractors are caricatures.

options: Use the client’s previous numerical score as the current score during turning
Use heart rate as the sole pain measure
Use the family’s description of usual comfort without observing the client during care
Use an appropriate behavioural tool and collateral history
why: The new behaviour needs current assessment rather than copying a previous score.
Physiological changes are nonspecific and may be absent.
Collateral history helps but should be combined with current structured observation.
Observed behaviours and known baseline can indicate pain when speech is limited.

items.assessment: An alert person who can point can still self-report. Visual scale is a meaningful alternative to behavioural-only or proxy assessment; the key is appropriately first-line.
New site and burning quality need a separate assessment; the prior knee diagnosis cannot explain them. Key does not prematurely diagnose neuropathy.
The selected goal directly reflects the client’s chosen function and acceptable symptoms. Medication-taking and zero-pain goals are plausible but less patient-centred outcome measures.
Correct graded shared plan, but never-hurts and coercion make answer obvious by tone.
issues: Correct graded shared plan, but never-hurts and coercion make answer obvious by tone.

options: Describe the usual benefits of exercise without asking what pain the client anticipates
Ask the client to complete the full planned session before deciding whether the fear was justified
Cancel all exercise until pain completely disappears
Explore the fear and plan a paced trial
why: General reassurance does not assess this client’s specific barrier.
An agreed paced trial is safer and more acceptable than using full-session completion as a prerequisite for discussion.
Avoidance may worsen deconditioning without resolving fear.
Collaboration addresses anticipation while respecting movement limits.

items.assessment: Timing, triggers, associated symptoms and treatment response provide useful diary data; selectively recording one worst episode or an isolated score omits relevant pattern information.
Burning during prescribed cold therapy warrants removal and inspection before continuing or changing layers. A prescribed duration does not override a new tissue-warning symptom.
Correct avoidance of heat injury, but high setting and thick blanket are weak compared with common supposedly safe workarounds.
issues: Correct avoidance of heat injury, but high setting and thick blanket are weak compared with common supposedly safe workarounds.

options: Assess sensation and choose a safer comfort plan
Use the lowest setting for the usual prescribed interval without checking sensation
Ask the client to remove it when too hot
Place a towel over the heating pad and rely on the client to report discomfort
why: Reduced sensation can prevent recognition of heat injury.
A low setting does not remove burn risk when protective sensation is impaired.
The client may not reliably feel excessive heat.
A barrier does not make impaired sensation a reliable way to regulate exposure.

items.assessment: The preferred adjunct is appropriate; replacing all treatment and disregarding preference are implausible.
issues: The preferred adjunct is appropriate; replacing all treatment and disregarding preference are implausible.

options: Continue imagery because it is commonly recommended
Schedule the music only after the client has attempted guided imagery
Choose a standard relaxation recording without asking which music the client finds comfortable
Offer preferred music as an adjunct
why: A disliked intervention may increase frustration rather than comfort.
Requiring a disliked strategy first ignores a feasible preferred adjunct.
The client’s preference should guide an acceptable intervention.
A chosen acceptable strategy is more likely to support relaxation.

items.assessment: Predictable procedural timing is important for anticipatory relief; daily totals or selected low scores can hide under-treated activity pain. No unsupported drug timing or dosing is imposed.
Nonverbal stiffening during touch warrants stopping and clarifying preference; lighter pressure alone does not resolve possible withdrawal of consent.
Targeting food odours is correct, but omitting oral care and pressuring intake are weak unrelated alternatives.
issues: Targeting food odours is correct, but omitting oral care and pressuring intake are weak unrelated alternatives.

options: Offer tolerated low-odour foods in a ventilated setting
Provide larger hot meals less often
Serve the usual hot meal covered, then uncover it fully at the bedside
Use a strongly scented room freshener before delivering meals
why: This reduces the identified stimulus while supporting intake.
Hot food odours and large portions may worsen symptoms.
Uncovering a hot meal may still expose the client to the identified odour trigger.
Another strong odour may worsen nausea instead of reducing the trigger.

items.assessment: For a weak actively vomiting client unable to turn, safe side/upright assistance protects the airway ahead of measuring emesis or detailed history. The exact position is appropriately individualized.
Two obvious staff-centred negatives create a weak SATA. Use narrow but plausible incomplete assessments.
issues: Two obvious staff-centred negatives create a weak SATA. Use narrow but plausible incomplete assessments.

options: Assess only sleepiness after medication, without checking physical needs
Assess only whether the same behaviour occurred yesterday, without examining the client now
Toileting need and abdominal fullness
Skin pressure and positioning
why: Medication effects may matter, but a restricted assessment can miss toileting or pressure discomfort.
Prior behaviour does not exclude a new treatable source of discomfort.
Elimination discomfort can present as restlessness.
Mechanical discomfort may drive repeated shifting.

items.assessment: The strongest-available-sedative and tolerate-less-sleep options are caricatures.
issues: The strongest-available-sedative and tolerate-less-sleep options are caricatures.

options: A fixed early bedtime for every client
Usual routine and daytime sleep pattern
Ask for a sleep medicine before reviewing the long afternoon naps
Schedule an earlier bedtime without asking about the client’s usual routine
why: A generic schedule may conflict with established habits.
The pattern may explain reduced night-time sleep drive.
Assess the sleep-wake pattern and modifiable contributors before medication selection.
A generic earlier bedtime may not address reduced sleep drive after lengthy naps.

items.assessment: Escalation is appropriate, but earplugs-only and afternoon naps are unrelated to new nocturnal breathlessness.
issues: Escalation is appropriate, but earplugs-only and afternoon naps are unrelated to new nocturnal breathlessness.

options: Assess the respiratory change and escalate
Offer a sleep aid as the first response
Add more pillows and document improved comfort without assessing the change
Record the awakenings as insomnia and discuss sleep hygiene at the next routine visit
why: Sleep interruption may reflect worsening cardiopulmonary status.
Sedation does not address the possible physiological cause.
Positioning may relieve symptoms but should not replace assessment of a new cardiopulmonary change.
Breathing-related awakenings need physiological assessment, not an insomnia label alone.

items.assessment: Large meal and daytime bed rest have little relation to the observed acoustic cause.
issues: Large meal and daytime bed rest have little relation to the observed acoustic cause.

options: Move the bedtime two hours earlier
Offer earplugs without discussing whether the client can hear needed alarms or communication
Cluster all care but leave avoidable hallway conversation unchanged
Reduce nearby noise and offer acceptable sound protection
why: Earlier sleep does not remove hallway noise.
Sound protection should be acceptable and safe for the individual setting.
Clustering may help other interruptions but does not address the main identified disturbance.
This directly addresses the identified disturbance.

items.assessment: Compatible clustering and moving suitable tasks earlier preserve sleep while maintaining required monitoring. Negatives reflect common uncoordinated scheduling and unauthorized omission.
Moving stimulant intake earlier and evaluating response is a specific reasonable trial. Caffeinated substitution and compensatory naps do not remove the likely trigger.

Painful CPAP marks require fit/interface assessment; tighter straps or unapproved padding can worsen pressure/leak. Acceptance of withdrawal remains subject to informed refusal, but discussing alternatives is appropriate.
Comfort-focused positioning is appropriate; stopping all assessment and analgesia solely to enforce routine are too blatant.
issues: Comfort-focused positioning is appropriate; stopping all assessment and analgesia solely to enforce routine are too blatant.

options: Continue large turns on a rigid schedule
Use a pressure-redistributing mattress and omit assessment of the discomfort during positioning
Repeat the same large turn after an analgesic without asking whether the client prefers smaller shifts
Agree on tolerated small changes and reassess
why: A fixed routine may impose disproportionate distress.
A mattress does not replace attention to comfort and skin response.
Analgesia may help, but the agreed plan should reflect tolerance and goals, not assume the original movement must continue.
Comfort goals and tissue tolerance should guide individual positioning.

items.assessment: The core explanation is humane and safe, but refusing discussion and compulsory portions are caricatures.
issues: The core explanation is humane and safe, but refusing discussion and compulsory portions are caricatures.

options: Present artificial feeding as the expected next step before discussing the client’s wishes
Set a calorie target for the family to meet before exploring the client’s comfort
Offer desired intake as tolerated and discuss comfort goals
Describe reduced intake only as a nutritional deficit that must be corrected
why: The benefits, burdens and goals need individual discussion; escalation is not automatic.
An imposed target may increase distress and ignores the dying person’s preferences.
Reduced intake may accompany dying; comfort guides support.
Reduced intake during dying should be discussed in the context of comfort, wishes and the whole clinical situation.

items.assessment: Supported forward sitting is appropriate, but lying flat and removing support to strengthen muscles are overtly wrong.
issues: Supported forward sitting is appropriate, but lying flat and removing support to strengthen muscles are overtly wrong.

options: Focus only on the saturation number
Support the position and reassess comfort
Change to the unit’s standard upright posture despite the client preferring the supported forward position
Document relief but remove the arm support when the client rests
why: Subjective distress matters even when saturation is unchanged.
An individually helpful supported posture can reduce effort.
Standard posture should not override a safe individually relieving position without clinical reason.
The arm support is part of the helpful position and should not be removed without reassessing effect.

items.assessment: Assessing separate symptom benefit is useful; replacing all analgesia and accusing inconsistency are weak.
issues: Assessing separate symptom benefit is useful; replacing all analgesia and accusing inconsistency are weak.

options: The intervention improved one agreed symptom
The strategy failed because pain was unchanged
Reduce prescribed analgesia without reviewing the persistent pain
Record only the unchanged pain score because tension is not part of comfort assessment
why: A reduced tension response is a meaningful separate outcome.
Comfort includes more than pain intensity alone.
Reduced anxiety does not establish adequate analgesia or authorize a dose change.
The intervention targeted procedural anxiety, so tension is a relevant separate outcome.

items.assessment: Meaningful-activity pacing is sound, but cancelling the call for staff routines is an obvious ethical cue.
issues: Meaningful-activity pacing is sound, but cancelling the call for staff routines is an obvious ethical cue.

options: Complete the full morning hygiene routine before the call because hygiene is normally scheduled first
Ask the family to reschedule the call without first discussing the client’s priorities
Combine bathing and the call so both are completed during the same energy period
Prioritize the meaningful activity with rest around it
why: A fixed task sequence may exhaust capacity for the client’s chosen activity.
Planning should begin with the client’s valued activity and available energy.
Simultaneous demands may undermine participation and comfort; individualized pacing is preferable.
Energy conservation should support the client's own priorities.

sourceVerificationLimit: Pain, sleep, CPAP and end-of-life claims were clinically reasoned but not individually externally checked in this batch; report is not clinical validation.
